title: Helix-stripe cowl
subtitle: A seamless spiral stripe cowl with no jogs at the colour changes.
excerpt: A cowl knitted in the round in two-colour helix stripes on 5 mm needles with worsted-weight yarn, finishing at 55 cm circumference and 28 cm tall. Helix knitting staggers two separate yarn balls so the stripes spiral continuously around the cowl without a visible jog at the round join. Each ball is worked alternately every two rounds.
sourceNotes: Helix stripe knitting in the round is documented in Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938), citations only, as a method of working spiral stripes without the jog produced by traditional round-based striping. The technique is in common use in modern knitting.
heroPrompt: A finished helix-stripe cowl in two-tone russet and gold worsted-weight yarn, photographed from above on a flat surface showing the continuous spiral stripe running without interruption around the tube.

glossaryTerms.definition: A method of working two-colour stripes in the round using two separate yarn balls, each attached at a point roughly opposite the other on the needle. The two yarns are picked up alternately every two rounds, producing a continuous spiral without a jog at the round boundary.
The visible step that occurs at the beginning of a new round when changing colour in standard striped in-the-round knitting. Helix technique eliminates the jog by staggering the two yarn positions.
Knitting a small circumference in the round on one long circular needle by pulling a loop of cable through the stitches at the halfway point.
A cast-on forming a neat elastic edge by using the tail and working yarn over two fingers simultaneously.

content.text: This is a cowl knitted in the round in two-colour
helix stripes
on 5 mm needles with worsted-weight yarn, finishing at 55 cm circumference and 28 cm tall. In standard striped in-the-round knitting a visible
jog

steps up at the round marker every time the colour changes. Helix knitting eliminates this by attaching each yarn at the halfway point of the previous yarn's stretch, so the two yarns spiral continuously without ever meeting at the same point of the round.
In-the-round construction is essential for helix striping; the technique does not translate to flat knitting. The
magic loop
on an 80 cm circular needle handles the 100 cast-on stitches comfortably. Each yarn ball needs about 130 m (approximately 80 g) of worsted-weight yarn.
What you need

items.name: Worsted-weight yarn, colour A
items.substitutions: Any worsted-weight yarn. Medium contrast gives a clear spiral; close tones give a tweed-like blend.

items.name: Stitch markers
items.qty: 2 (of different colours, one for round start, one for colour B join)

content.text: Gauge

18 sts x 24 rounds = 10 x 10 cm in stocking stitch in the round on 5 mm needles, blocked. The helix stripe fabric knits at the same gauge as plain stocking stitch. One stitch per 10 cm off gauge shifts the finished circumference by approximately 3 cm at this stitch count.
Pattern
Cast on and set up
Use the
long-tail cast-on

in colour A to place 100 stitches on the needle. Before beginning, calculate the tail: tail_cm = (needle circumference mm x stitch count) / 10 + 15. For 5 mm needles (circumference approximately 15.7 mm) and 100 stitches: (15.7 x 100) / 10 + 15 = 157 + 15 = 172 cm. Leave at least 172 cm of colour A tail.

Stitch count check-in: after the cast-on you should have 100 stitches on the needle. Join to work in the round. Place the round-start marker. Work 2 rounds in colour A only (stocking stitch, all K). At the start of round 3, work the first 50 stitches in colour A, then place the colour B marker. Attach colour B at this point and knit the remaining 50 stitches. Colour A is now at the round-start marker; colour B is at the halfway marker.
Body

From this point, the two yarns alternate every 50 stitches. Work to the colour B marker in colour A (knit all stitches), slip marker, pick up colour B, knit to the round-start marker, slip marker, pick up colour A. The two join points are staggered by 50 stitches, so the stripes spiral without meeting at the same spot.
Continue until the cowl measures 28 cm from the cast-on. At the halfway mark (approximately round 34 as counted from each yarn's own progress), count your stitches.
Stitch count check-in: at the halfway mark you should have 100 stitches on the needle.
Bind off

Work a stretchy bind-off using whichever colour is at the round-start marker. The bind-off will create a slight colour imbalance at the edge; this is normal in helix knitting and is barely visible once the edge is worn.
Common faults

Picking up the wrong colour at a join. The two yarns can swing across the needle when working quickly. Before picking up each yarn, confirm it is the colour that has been resting since the previous join rather than the one just used. The resting yarn has a slight tension on it from the last stitch it worked.

Twisting the two yarns around each other at the join. Unlike traditional colour joining, helix yarn balls should NOT be twisted around each other at the join. Simply drop one and pick up the other; twisting creates tangles after a few rounds.

Visible loose stitch at the join. The first stitch after picking up a resting yarn can be loose because the resting yarn has relaxed. Pull the resting yarn gently before knitting the first stitch to tighten the previous stitch in that yarn.
Finishing
Weave in all tails: the cast-on tail from colour A, the join tail from colour B, and the bind-off tail. Block by wetting and drying over a round form to even out the helix.
Care
Handwash in cool water with wool wash. Lay flat or over a round form to dry.
What to try next

The two-colour ribbed cowl works two colours in the round using full rounds of each colour rather than a helix, making clean horizontal stripes. The gradient scarf adds three or more colours across a single flat piece using the same alternating-yarn technique worked flat.
